utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd remind you of the affirmation you made which still applies, and Mr. Djordjevic will continue his questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we resume, I'd like to clarify an answer I made at the very end of yesterday's session if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you asked me about the various projects that our Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project had undertaken. The projects involving the lodge owned by the Serbian Orthodox Church at Velika Hoca and the kulas, we were involved with Cultural Heritage Without Borders in the planning stages, but the actual funding for the reconstruction itself came from the Swedish International Development Agency and the European Commission. So I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yesterday we heard about the Swedish foundation. You said that you had received funds for reconstruction of your projects with them. I'm interested in the following: Since we heard there were problems, Mr. Riedlmayer, for the restoration of the church in Drsnik because the Orthodox priests there asked that it be done together with the patriarchy in Belgrade or the authorities in Belgrade, and you said that the mosque was restored, and what I'm interested in -- I assume that the mosque was restored in agreement with the Islamic Community in Kosovo. Is this correct, and can we agree with this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know, are you aware of the reasons, why there were no negotiations with the patriarchy of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Belgrade? Do you have any information about that in relation to the restoration of the Drsnik monastery or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Our initial contacts were with Father Savo Janjic and Petar Ulemek of the Orthodox Eparchy of Raska and Prizren. And things looked promising and then certain conditions kept coming up about working with the Serbian Institute for the Protection of Monuments and UNMIK, the UN Mission, insisted that it had to be done through the UNMIK authorities. And at that point we stepped back and I don't know where the negotiations further went. At that point I was no longer in Kosovo, and some of that contact was carried out by Mr. Herscher. But all of the projects were administratively complicated by conflicting constituencies and bureaucratic difficulties, including the mosque project. It took twice as long as we had originally thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question refers to your associate and colleague Herscher. Am I correct if I were to conclude that the work that you did, you mentioned the Kosovska Mitrovica area and the library in the southern part of Kosovska Mitrovica, was something that you did pro bono, not under a specific agreement or a contract, while Mr. Herscher was at some post in the UNMIK institutions? And if he was, can you please clarify for us what that was.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. At that point Mr. Herscher was not yet employed by UNMIK. I received a special mission from the UNMIK Department of Culture to carry out this inspection of the library. There had previously been a mission from the International Federation of Library Associations in Mitrovica to carry out the survey of the library, and this was a follow-up mission. And basically UNMIK agreed to pay for my hotel. Otherwise, I received no honourarium. I spent the day in Mitrovica, wrote my report, and then the following day returned to the United States. It merely extended my stay in Kosovo by one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Herscher, what will his post be later in UNMIK? What will his post be?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a -- received a six-month contract later that year to be assistant head of the Department of Culture of the UN Mission in Kosovo. Subsequently when the previous head left for a while, he was acting head. Then he returned to the United States and began his teaching career. And subsequently I understand he worked as a consultant for UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Together with Mr. Herscher you wrote a work named "Monument and Crime"; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when this study or work was published and what was its main topic? What do you exactly deal with in this work that you did jointly with Mr. Herscher?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This article appeared in a cultural theory journal called "Grey Room." I believe it appeared in the autumn of 2001. I don't have my CV in front of me. And it was -- consisted of an essay and a series of photographs, and the essay dealt with the various significations of architecture in Kosovo and how they were used in various political arguments concerning the status of Kosovo. The article, I assume, has been made available to you. It's been some years since I've read it last. If you have specific questions about it, I would be glad to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I found this article myself and I read it, but I would like to hear from you about certain political observations that you referred to there in relation to the destruction of cultural monuments in Kosovo and the cultural heritage of Kosovo. Which monuments were the main topic of observation in your article? Were they the monuments of all cultures in a multi-ethnic approach, or was it an article related to the Islamic culture, which, as you said yourself, was your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, the article dealt with all the elements of culture in Kosovo, but it was not meant to be a survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the objective?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article was invited to the journal which dealt with issues of cultural theory and representation, and part of the argument of the article was that cultural heritage is not by its nature something that is detached from political events and political views, that it can be used to promote political arguments or neglected in the service of political arguments. As I say, it's been a while, so if you would like to quote something I can respond to it; but in general terms this is what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to be dwelling on this anymore. Thank you for your reply, and it will be very useful to read that essay of yours. But am I correct if I were to say that you also published together a work "Burned Books and Scattered Relics." Am I correct if I say that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The article "Burned Books and Blasted Shrines" was something that appeared in a UNESCO Courier. It was an interview, and a very short piece, one-page long. I assume that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, are you able to remember the main topic of that article or that interview?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview, as far as I recall, merely asked very briefly about our mission in Kosovo and what our findings were. It was a short oral summary. I was interviewed by telephone from UNESCO's Paris headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now something about the Packard Institute, which you mentioned was one of the donors and that they financed the entire thing, that you had contacted them. And I heard during the examination-in-chief by my learned friend Ms. Kravetz something about that. However, making inquiries about the Packard Institute, I found on the institute's web page something which I would like you to clarify for me. What I found was that the Packard Institute does not finance projects from others. They do not provide funds for projects of others, but finance only projects it considers to be their own. So the project that you were involved with in Kosovo, was that a Packard project and that's why it received financing, or was this some kind of exception; and if it was, can you please explain what this is about.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first explain about the Packard Humanities Institute. The name Packard relates, originally, to one of the founders of the famous Hewlett-Packard computer company, but the person who founded and runs that institute is the son of that founder. He has no connection with the company. He is a retired professor of classics and has various cultural interests. He supports archaeological excavations in Greece, Albania, Turkey, various publishing ventures, and so forth. I know the web site to which you refer. It is meant as a way of deterring people from barraging them with project proposals. Like many private foundations in the US, the way the Packard Humanities Institute works is that projects are referred to them by people they trust, by sort of an advisory board. And earlier, before the Kosovo project was conceived, I had had contact with the Packard Humanities Institute already concerning projects involving reconstruction of manuscript libraries in Bosnia. They had at that time considered and then decided not to support the initiative, but that established the contact. And so when we came up with this Kosovo Cultural Heritage Project, I used that contact to personally approach the people at the institute and ask if they would be interested in funding it. And after some time they said yes. Under very restricted circumstances. We had money, only a certain amount of money only for a certain amount of time, and not renewable. So I guess you could qualify it as an exception. But the web site notwithstanding, the projects that they do fund, they don't manage them out of the Packard Humanities Institute. These are projects run by other people, and they provide the funding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The founders of the Packard Foundation are Mr. Packard and his wife. Who manages the institute, as for that, I didn't know that it was the son, I didn't find that on the web site. But on the web site I found other links that direct to the separate or special projects of the Packard institute you spoke about, the archaeological excavations, and the financing of such projects. I did find that. But this project about the damage to the cultural heritage in Kosovo is something that I did not find on any of the links of this institution. Very well, I understand you explained that it was an exception. The next question for you is that you spent some considerable time of your examination-in-chief in explaining that you worked independently, you were not so connected with The Hague Tribunal OTP at that time, that it was simply a project of yours, for which I see that was supported by Harvard, if I understood that correctly. So could you explain that part as well. And finally, the project is, in essence, your project and the project of Mr. Herscher; am I correct when I conclude this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. First of all, under American law a charitable institution, such as the Packard Foundation cannot easily give out money to individuals acting on their own, they have to channel the money through another non-profit institution. So we arranged for a centre at Harvard to act as the disburser of the funds; however, the project itself was not a project of Harvard University. It was a project of the two principal researchers, Mr. Herscher and myself. When I worked on the Kosovo project, I was on vacation from my Harvard job. It's not that they were paying me to do this. So the connection with Harvard was essentially a nominal one. Does that answer your question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the last thing I said in my question or the conclusion with which I think you will agree. It was a project of you and your partner in the project, and Mr. Herscher; am I correct when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question -- well, I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I'm going to do my best today -- well, I'm trying all the time to take into consideration everything that you said in the Milutinovic case. This is something that is already in the case file of this case, and I'm just going to then ask you about things that were not clarified in that case as it relates to your testimony or your statement. So one of the things dealt with by my colleagues, which I personally believe was not clarified completely, is the way in which you drafted the report, which we all have, and it implies evidence or records with photographs of the damaged buildings. There is also a section in which you talk about the eye-witnesses or people who are sources of all types of information. What I would like to ask you is this. You say that it's your project. Did you set yourself the task, number one, to note the damage in the objects that are part of the cultural heritage of Kosovo -- well, this is clear to me. But did you also set a task for yourself to establish the causes of the damage and who caused the damage? Because in the reply that you gave to my learned friend during the examination-in-chief, you said, among other things, that we took those statements in order to assist the Court. Now, this is not clear to me. First of all, up until that time I had one opinion; after that, I had a different opinion. So just explain to me what was your task in relation to this second item? It's clear to me in relation to the first item, but what was your task in assisting the Court to acquire information on the manner in which the damage was caused on these cultural monuments? Did you do something in order to acquire that knowledge? How was the work organised?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the preliminary section of our report, it states that what prompted our report was the number of allegations that surfaced during and immediately after the war regarding the destruction of cultural monuments. We set out to investigate these allegations in their fullness in the sense that we wanted to know: Had these monuments been damaged; and if so, when and how. And the damage of who damaged it, we were limited in our capability so as to determine that. But to the extent that we acquired information that would point in that direction, we felt obliged to record it. The manner in which we recorded it was designed to aid anyone who was pursuing an investigation of who was responsible, to then proceed with those leads. But obviously we are not criminal investigators. The conclusions we can draw ourselves have to do with things like: What is the condition of the building? What might have caused the building to be in the condition that it is in? And more general ones about patterns of destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I were to say that your investigation was limited only to the period you refer to in your report immediately after the KFOR forces entered Kosovo, therefore, after June? So the period that you spent in Kosovo and Metohija and inspected 144 monuments. I think you mentioned that figure. Can you please tell me exactly how much time did you spend in Kosovo? Did you go there on several occasions when you were writing the report with Dr. -- Mr. Herscher or did you -- did your stay precede the writing of the actual report and how much time in total did you spend in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. As I have indicated, I believe during the direct examination, I -- Mr. Herscher and I went to Kosovo three times. The first time was in October of 1999, when we spent most of the month there, approximately three and a half weeks; the second time was three weeks in the following October, October of 2000; and the last time was in March and April of 2001, again for about three weeks. The amount of time that we spent on each monument varied, obviously. If a monument had been completely destroyed, there wasn't a lot to do other than take a picture and walk the site. If it was a more complex one, we would spend considerable time. The greatest amount of time was taken up by travelling, because even though Kosovo is a small place, the infrastructure was in very bad shape. So we spent enormously long days, usually leaving before daylight and returning long after dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, while you were in Kosovo, were you stationed in one place only or did you travel around and stayed wherever the subject of your interest was?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That varied according to our visit. The first time around we were based in Pristina and took long day-trips out of Pristina. The second and third trip we stayed not only in Pristina but also in Pec, in western Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is as follows. You mentioned the time-limit and your time constraints with reference to your report and you also mentioned the bad shape of roads in Kosovo. How did you make arrangements for your travels to the sites that you wanted to visit? Did you have any security detail with you or did you arrange that ad hoc together with UNMIK authorities or did you organise it by yourself on an ad hoc basis?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no prior contact with UNMIK authorities or anyone else in that sense. We hired a car and driver. The car and driver was recommended to me by somebody I knew who was a reporter who had used the same driver before. What helped matters is that the driver was bilingual. He new Turkish as well as Albanian. And so I was able to use his services as an interpreter in cases where I couldn't speak to people directly. We hired him on a daily basis and paid him off at the end of each day, and I think at the end of the trip he had ruined his car but had enough money to buy a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that before each trip you went either to the offices of the Prosecution or UNMIK - please remind me what you said - in order to acquire information about your destination and to investigate about the security situation with regard to your forthcoming trip. Since I didn't realise from that record where you got this information, for example, when you spoke about Mitrovica you said you weren't going there because of the riots there on the river Ibar.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was our sole contact with the UNMIK field -- I'm sorry, with the ICTY field office in Pristina. The ICTY field office would, on a daily basis, receive a security report from KFOR, the NATO authorities, and they encouraged us in advance of each day's trip to check with them on what the daily forecast was for security environment. And in most cases there was no problem. On that particular day, we were warned not to go to Mitrovica and so we didn't. We didn't inform them actually where we were going. We just asked for the copy of the daily security report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: With your previous answer you just responded to how it worked on the road. As I understand, this translation from English into Turkish and Albanian, vice versa, can you explain in more detail how this was achieved because you had a person, as you said, who was your field translator.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically on each expedition we would have our driver, we would have Mr. Herscher and myself, and on various occasions we took people with us to act as guides. For example, somebody from the Institute for the Protection of Monuments. The language aspect of it worked the following way: I am fluent in a number of languages, including German and Turkish. I'm fluent in Turkish in part because I spent three years in Turkey on a Fulbright. In Kosovo there are lots of people who have worked in Switzerland and Germany and speak German, so the German helped in those cases. And in the cities such as Prizren, to a certain extent in Vucitrn, Mitrovica, and Pristina, you will find a lot of people who also know Turkish. I even spoke with Serbs who knew Turkish. It was what people in the cities had as a skill. So that worked for a communication. Occasionally we would be in a situation where the person only knew Albanian. In that case we asked -- I would speak Turkish to our driver, and our driver would translate from Albanian and Turkish and back. So there was only one language. So it wasn't English to Turkish to Albanian; it was just -- I spoke Turkish, he translated into Turkish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At this. This translator and driver of yours, was he a driver by profession or did he have some other occupation?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By occupation he had been before the war a musician and had performed on Pristina Radio, and he had travelled throughout Kosovo giving concerts so he was familiar with the roads and he had a car, which was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report drafted in 2001, you speak, inter alia, about the Kosovo Institute for Protection of Monuments, the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of the then-Yugoslavia. But what I'm interested in is that in one of the paragraphs you say that the criteria that the Yugoslav authorities applied when they compiled a list of monuments to be protected were conditioned to a great extent or dependent to a great extent on political reasoning. Since you have a university degree in social sciences, I would like to ask you what was your meaning by saying that? And then depending on your answer I would move on to my next question, which is related to this one. But before that can I have your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The reference was to the legislation which was enacted to declare certain monuments and sites to be under legal protection. This kind of protection legislation exists in most countries of the world at various levels, either local or national, and usually entitles the monument to a degree of protection in the sense that destruction or alteration of the monument without permission is prohibited and monuments become eligible for certain degrees of restoration assistance from the central government. Now, the criteria in all cases represent a judgement as to what is important and worthy of preserving. And while certain of the criteria are universal and sensible, is this a monument of great age? Is it connected with some important historic event? Is it something that has gained universal admiration and is represented in the literature, in the professional literature? But to another extent, the -- especially the funding aspect of it which is closely linked to the designation has to do with what a government, what an authority, considers to be a priority. So, for example, during the times of communist Yugoslavia, the greatest attention was paid to memorials of the Second World War and of the Partizan movement, and every -- for example, in Kosovo -- in addition to the museum of Kosovo, all of the local museums had as one of their principal tasks preserving and exhibiting elements of the Partizan movement. So in the same sense the determination of what to designate and what not to designate was not merely a neutral decision. It had to do with what was considered politically important as well. And what I was referring to in the report, and I assume what you are referring to here, is the fact that although Kosovo has many monuments of great age, both Islamic and Orthodox, very few Islamic monuments had been designated to be under protection, whereas a greater number of monuments had gone under protection that were of the Orthodox heritage. And this is also reflected in the amount of money that was then subsequently spent on restoration efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: Are you aware that back in 1977 the Law on the Protection of Cultural Heritage was passed, referring to the then-autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, and this is a period that the Albanian population claimed to be the period of their highest autonomy enjoyed by them. Do you know that all the employees of the institute, including the director, were ethnic Albanians? And I'm talking about the Institute for the Protection of Monuments. And do you know how -- what provisions this law made concerning the protection of monuments in Kosovo? Do you know how many Serbian Orthodox monuments have been placed under protection under this specific law? Can I first have this answer, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I'm aware of -- that the legislation was passed. I do not know the composition of the staff of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in the 1970s, however I'm aware of what it was in the 1990s, in which period it was not majority Albanian. As to the numbers of monuments that were placed under protection, my understanding is that this varied from year to year because additional monuments were added at very points, and so I don't have an exact figure. There were some figures from the period under investigation, namely, the status quo of the 1990s, which we derived from publications. We did not have access to the full register. And they are cited in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In that period, many more monuments of the Serbian Orthodox Church enjoyed protection. Now, apart from the ideological reasons, do you know what else guided the government in providing funds for the protection? Do you know which specific criteria have been laid down when it comes to the protection of cultural monuments, for example, sacral monuments, do you know exactly what criteria were in place because they are very specifically listed in the law. And I am talking about the criteria that would determine that -- for a specific monument to be placed under protection.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to what guided the allocation of funds, I assume the primary consideration was budgetary priorities. And I know that in much of the latter period of the former Yugoslavia, money was very tight. And so protections that were on the books did not necessarily result in allocations of necessary funds. As to the specific aspects of the law, I have not read the legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is a general one. Are you aware today of, first of all, the criteria being applied by the UNESCO? We know what is the agenda of this UN agency, in order to declare a certain cultural asset the world heritage? So can you tell us about the UNESCO criteria that determine how certain monuments are being designated?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, and this really steps beyond my particular expertise, is that the nominations for a site to be -- or monument to be entered on the World Heritage List are submitted by the national UNESCO committees to the world heritage section of UNESCO in Paris, and that it takes a fairly long process for UNESCO to arrive at such a designation. I also know that in the case of the former Yugoslavia before the year 2000 there were very few World Heritage Sites, one of them being Dubrovnik, another being some Serbian monasteries in the Sandzak reason, but that before 2004, I believe, there were no designated World Heritage Sites either in Kosovo or in Bosnia for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that you're not familiar with the explicit criteria applied by UNESCO in the process of assigning a certain monument the title of the World Heritage Site. However, my next question is as follows. We're now in the year 2009. Do you know at present how many monuments there are in Kosovo from the Serbian cultural media that are considered World Heritage Site, and how many monuments of the Serbian Orthodox Church are declared World Heritage Sites? Are there any Roman Catholic sites that are given this title or any other building or site, whether it be sacral or religious, that enjoys this status at present?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I haven't been keeping track of this as much as perhaps I should have, but my understanding is that the monastery at Visoki Decani was the first to get that designation. And then the Bogorodica Ljeviska church in Prizren and Gracanica monastery and, I believe, the Pec Patriarchate, so that makes four, I believe. I'm not aware of others, but I may be mistaken. As far as Roman Catholic churches, none are World Heritage Sites. There are a few of great antiquity in Kosovo that are still standing. There are some medieval ruins. And none of the Islamic sites have been so designated, although there are some monuments of considerable antiquity and artistic importance. But as I said, prior to 2004 there were none of any category that had been so designated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. Do you think that the UNESCO experts were guided by political judgements when they afforded four Serbian monasteries the status of World Heritage Sites or were they guided by some other reasons after all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad that these got the designation. They are indeed great treasures of world art. I think it's indisputable. They're mentioned in all the art history books. They represent a very interesting moment in cultural history and are important, not only for the region or for Serbian culture, but also for world culture. I would not dispute that in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is indisputable. But I put a very specific question to you whether the UNESCO, as well, was guided by political reasons when they afforded these sites the status of extremely important World Heritage Sites.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not believe that it was a political decision at all. As I indicated in my earlier responses, there are certain monuments which, simply by their nature, are obvious candidates for protection because of their cultural importance, because of their age or historical significance. I think these are certainly among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We absolutely agree on this, Mr. Riedlmayer. My next question is as follows: In Kosovo, do you know which are the oldest mosques from which century that can really have a great historical value, bearing in mind the history that happened in that region and what is usually referred to as the traditional Islamic architecture? Can you tell me if there are any mosques of that kind, I think there are only a few of them, but I would like to hear the answer from you because you are an expert in this area.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fair question. The earliest mosques in Kosovo that are still existent are from the fifteenth century. They include, among others, the Bajrakli xhamija in Pec of which we saw a picture during the direct examination. They include the Careva [phoen] xhamija, the Emperor's mosque in Pristina. And then there is a ruined mosque near Strpce, near a village called Mazgit, which dates from that period but is in -- not a well-preserved state. Prizren has more than 30 different mosques, and it -- many of them dating from the 15th and 16th centuries, and it has been designated as a site of unusual importance by the World Monuments Fund. And there are also a number of other mosques in smaller locations in Kosovo, such as the mosque in Rogovo, the Hadum mosque in Djakovica, which is now undergoing further restoration under UNESCO auspices. And in addition to the mosques, there are also other Islamic monuments like the hammam in Prizren and so forth. So indeed Kosovo has some monuments of the Islamic tradition that are 500 or more years old and some of them are of cultural importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. To the best of my knowledge, the oldest monuments of that nature date from the sixteenth century and this is the information that I acquired by relying on various sources in the literature. However, since the purpose of my examination -- of my cross-examination is not this subject. My next question will be - and I kindly ask you to bear with me a little until I move to my next topic. This is another general topic, and it refers to the methodology of collecting information. I would like to notice that when you made inquiries about the damage inflicted on the Serbian Orthodox sacral monuments you mainly interviewed the clergy or the Serbs living in the area and with whom you have an opportunity to contact. You mentioned Father Savo Janjic, et cetera. When you inquired about how the damage was caused to both the civilian and sacral monuments of the Islamic culture, however, you mainly talked to the Albanians. However, when we are talking about the St. Anton church, the Catholic church, you talked about it also with the priest of that church. So you do realise that my question is primarily aimed at this methodology that you applied in collecting what I would call additional information relating to the cause of damage relating to the perpetrators, their identity, and the way in which they caused the damage. Now, when you spoke about all these things, did you talk with the police? Did you talk with anyone from the international community present in Kosovo? Did you review any official information about this damage if any were available? Now, I think this is a compound question, and I'm going to stop now.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I can sort it out. As to who our informants were, we got our information on this category of information -- I'm sorry, from wherever we could get it. For example, you mention the destruction of -- I'm sorry, the destruction of the Serbian monasteries. We spoke to the clergy because the clergy had collected a lot of information and they were very active in publicising it. And so it seemed like a natural way to go. Similarly, in the case of St. Anthony's Catholic church in Djakovica, I arrived at the church looking for signs of damage because it had been one of the allegations listed in the Yugoslav White Book. When I arrived there, I was pleased to find that the priest of the church, Father Ambroz Ukaj, was present at the church, and furthermore, that he spoke fluent Turkish. And so we spent about 45 minutes to an hour in conversation and he told me that he had actually been in Djakovica during the war. So he seemed to me to be an informant who had some valuable information to provide. Now, as to police, when we were there in October of 1999, UNMIK police had to a great extent not really been established throughout Kosovo yet. They were still in the process of setting up. There were international policemen we met who had just arrived in Kosovo and who were still orienting themselves. They had no records. Things were in a fair state of chaos. It would not have been a productive use of our time to try to go down to police stations and ask for that kind of information, especially since that really was not the primary focus of our investigation. We were there to look at buildings. Now, let me see if there's anything else. International community, we tried to get information from the international community, and, to the extent that we could, we did get it. For example, in Pec there was a very energetic young French woman who was working for UNMIK who had organised a project to document the destruction of kulas. And so we got their figures, not the first time around while their survey was still in progress, but on our return trip to Kosovo. UNESCO at that point had only one person seconded to the UN administration, Mr. Mark Richmond his specialty was education, and he had no information to offer on monuments or sites and no knowledge of them. And similarly we tried without much success to get information from local authorities. The one exception was Djakovica which had its own municipal institute for the protection of monuments, and they were quite helpful in providing us with information about monuments in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Mr. Mark Richmond. He also had something to do, as far as I understood, with the allegations that something of the cultural heritage was destroyed -- or rather, was not destroyed. However, in your report you disputed his findings. Can you please tell me what actually this whole thing was about when we are talking about this person, this Mark Richmond.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do not recall what you are referring to. Can you quote it back to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Later, so we don't lose time because I have a lot of things to put to you, I will go back to that after the break so that we don't lose any time now. My following question has to do with the fact you say you were in one of the Serbian monasteries and that KFOR did not allow you to enter the monastery. Did I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was in Prizren, I believe. KFOR had surrounded the Serbian Orthodox patriarchate and its monastery in Prizren, and they didn't allow us in. I believe this is what you're referring to. On a subsequent visit, Mr. Herscher did go inside. But in October of 1999, they cited security reasons for not letting us in. Remember that we were there on our own. We had no institutional clout to throw at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, that is my next question. Were you staying as part of any institutions of the system and reported there about your area of work? Did you ever any special passes or did you experience what you experienced because your stay was an ad hoc trip as far as they were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you -- for this you have to understand the post-war situation in Kosovo. When we arrived in Kosovo we crossed over from Macedonia, which was the closest airport in Skopje, and we crossed at Jazince which is high up in the mountains. And it turned out we needed no papers other than to show our passports, which they checked against the list of presumably people who should not be admitted, we were not on it, and we were in -- no stamps, nothing. We arrived in Pristina and made some inquiries and found out that UNHCR was holding weekly conferences of NGOs that were interested in buildings of various sources. And so we attended those conferences. My sense was that UNHCR was essentially acting as a forum for sharing information, but they were not actively coordinating anything. And so to cut the story short, at that point anyone could be active as an NGO in Kosovo without going through great formalities. And we stayed there for a month without having to register with the police or having any official status whatsoever. When we were stopped at roadblocks, all we had to show was our identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This explains quite a lot. You mentioned a little while ago some civilian buildings, you mention the "konaks," the "hammams," and the last thing that you mentioned will be a brief topic of interest. These are the "kullas," or the towers. In your report you mentioned that the towers were a traditional type of building in Kosovo and in this part of the Balkans. I understand what you are trying to say when you say "in Kosovo," but I want to ask you what do you mean when you say "in this part of the Balkans"?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, the term "kula" simply means tower, and various structures that are called "kula" are found all the way from Dalmatia down to Greece. There is a very particular kind of construction, which is referred to in, for example, the Serbian literature as Siptarska Kula, the Albanian "kulla," which is found mainly in Kosovo and some adjacent areas of Macedonia and Montenegro. They used to be found in northern Albania as well, but most of them were demolished under the Enver Hoxha regime. So they were particular to that region and were mainly found in Kosovo. And in Kosovo they were concentrated in particular in the western part, the part in Serbia known as Metohija and in Albanian as the Plain of Dukagjini.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the translation that I see Metohija and Dukagjin is exactly the same area. Are we going to agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the word "kula"? Which language is that word appearing in primarily? Is it Albanian? Turkish? Serbian? Or any other language?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in all of the ones you mentioned plus several more. The root of the word I believe is Arabic, how -- and it just means "tower," but -- whether spelled with one L as in Serbian or with two L's as in Albanian. It is a building type that is know in the Balkans and were particularly constructed in the 18th and 19th centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The word "kula" does have Arabic origin -- is of Arabic origin; however, in Serbia when we used that word it is indicated as a word of Turkish origin, as a word that has been taken into the language from the Turkish language. And that is the reason when you say "kula" in the Serbian language we all have an idea of what you have just said. Yeah, we see that it represents a tower. I don't have any photographs, but perhaps we will have some later. But are you able to describe what a kula looks like in the western part of Kosovo? It is definitely a tower. What sort of a tower is it? What does it consist of? What is it built of? What is its height? Could you please describe it.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, a kula is constructed of stone. It is a fairly massive construction. I have read descriptions of how kulas were made, the last ones that were constructed at the end of World War II were these community projects where people would go out and collect stones from river-beds. And what they are -- they're not towers in the sense that most of them are not taller than they are wide, but they are unusually high for a region in which most houses are fairly low to the ground. They are usually two, in some cases three, or even four storeys high. The lower part of the kula is usually made of massive unfinished stones. The only finished stones are the ornamental entrance. And at the very top of the kula usually wrapped around one corner of the building is what's known in Albanian as "oda e burreve" the men's room or guest-room which is the fancy room of the house. This is where guests are received, where family councils meet. It has a fireplace. It has benches running around. The family usually lives in much plainer rooms on the floor immediately below the guest-room, and the bottom is where the animals and grain and agricultural tools are kept. So it's a development very much like many of the medieval houses in other parts of Europe. What's particular about the construction is that it is meant to provide both shelter and protection. They were built in the eighteenth and nineteenth century at a time when the area was very insecure. There were bandits, there were family feuds. So the bottom floor where the animals and the fodder were kept had no windows at all. The family areas had very small windows. And the only part that had substantial windows generally was the guest-room at the very top. Now, that's the typical rural kula. In the cities like Pec, there were also urban kula which had a much more urbane design with bigger windows. A typical example is the Kulla of Jashar Pasha in the centre of Pec which is also mentioned in my report. The kulas were generally owned by a single extended Albanian family. They would not necessarily all live within the same kula. Often members of the family would live in smaller houses nearby as part of a larger family compound. But even in modern times the kula was the centre of great family occasions such as weddings and funerals where they would all gather. Is that a sufficient description?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to ask to have on the monitor e-court evidence of the Defence and to show in order from D004-2844 to D004-2848. So can we look at these photographs one by one from 44 to 48, please, and can we please just stay five seconds on each photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to briefly comment. This is Bosnia, this is Bihac, Western Bosnia, and what we see here is the Dizdar Kula in the Belgrade fort, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the memorial kula erected near Pristina in Gazimestan. It's a monument to the fighters killed in the battle with the Turks in 1389.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a kula from Bosnia. And you see that it has a wooden roof that is constructed at the top, and it is located in Gradac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a kula in Istanbul.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question relating to all these kulas that you've seen, this one is in Turkey, and it was -- and the previous ones you saw are mostly in the Balkan area. None of them are from Kosovo. My next question is if any of the kulas that you've seen can be compared with any of the kulas that are in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no; not except in the most general of terms. "Kula," as we already discussed, is a generic word meaning "tower." One thing you did not show which exists in many cities in the Balkans is a Sahat Kula, a clock-tower, which are very slim and very tall. So any structure that is a tower and of a certain historic period can be and often is referred to as "kula." But not every kula, not every tower, belongs to this class of typical ethnic Albanian dwelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question is if you know that there were many kulas for which you claim were typically Albanian that were owned by Serbs, not only in cities.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I mention in my report that there were kulas owned by Serbs, and I also referred to the fact that these seemed to be the only kulas that escaped destruction. However, as I pointed out in my testimony in the Milutinovic case, among others, even the publications of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments of the Republic of Serbia in the 1990s included specific reference to the fact that these are typically Albanian dwellings. I refer, for example, to the article by Jovan Krunic, "Siptarska Kulla Metohije," the Albanian Towers of Metohija. So, yes, there was no law saying that every resident of every kula had to be an Albanian, but they were associated with Albanian culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could we connect them with the heritage that had to do with the 500-year-long stay of Turks in that area? You know when the Turks withdrew from that area, it was at the beginning of the twentieth century, actually, and in some places much later even.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they can be connected in two ways. One is as you state, the word "kula" is something that entered Balkan languages through Turkish, but so did three-quarters of the words on any recipe in the -- restaurant in the Balkans. But the other way it is, of course, that anything that happened during those 500 years is connected. However, I'm not aware, in spite of many Albanians' claims that "kullas" go back to antiquity, I am not aware of any kula that is older than the eighteenth century. These were essentially an architectural fashion that developed in the 1700s, peaked in the 1900s, and pretty much ceased by the middle of the twentieth century. So it is particular -- to a particular region and to a particular time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will agree with you that there is no kula in Kosovo that is older than the nineteenth century, actually, but I'm also going to agree with those Albanians who told you that the kulas existed there even before 500 years -- or 500 years earlier, or 400 years earlier. But what I want to ask you is of a completely different nature; it has to do with the facilities that were used for purposes of defence. Can you please tell us now because now we are talking about the Siptar, the Albanian "kullas," and this is something that Serb chroniclers also say, can you please tell us, in relation to the households, Albanian households, where would a kula be located in reference to a residential building of a regular Albanian household? You said that there's a residential part and the kulas were used for different ceremonial or special occasions, burials and celebrations, and so on. Where were they located in relation to the rest of the household?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, actually, I didn't say that people didn't live in kulas. People did live in kulas. The second floor was usually family living quarters. What I said is that they were -- as families grew and Kosovo is one of the last places where you had the traditional Balkan extended family, what's known in Serbian as "zadruga" where multiple generations of the same family lived together and shared their money and shared their work and child care and everything else. And so a compound might contain a monumental kula and several smaller buildings around it. And such a kula might be out in a village somewhere surrounded by smaller houses or there might be an aggregation of kulas. For example, there is a very famous village near Junik called Nivokaz which had 24 kulas all grouped together in a single village. So similarly, the old town of Decani had an enormous number of kulas which were laid out on streets. The kulas were right next to the street, and so they were like ordinary townhouses, but what this was was a large village of kulas. So not every one of them was an isolated compound in the country-side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question before the break, which is approaching is: When you said that -- you said that the kula in the ground floor they held cattle and the first floor was the residential area and the second floor was the best rooms where they had celebrations and special celebrations. Do you -- and you said that the kula, the purpose of it was for habitation and also defence. When you said that, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I pointed out, the kula arose at the time when order was breaking down in that region. In the eighteenth and nineteenth century there were a lot of bandi ts and a lot of blood-feuds. And kulas, because they were such massive structures, offered defence to the family if it was attacked, whether by bandits, by tax collectors, or by the rival family. So they could take shelter inside the windowless walls and they had enough provisions in the bottom level so they wouldn't have to necessarily go out for several days. So in that sense, yes, they had it as a defensive purpose. And because the windows were small, they weren't as vulnerable then as if they had had larger windows. And does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, would you agree with my conclusion that kulas at the time were a necessity, not a fashion trend, in late nineteenth century when such a large number of them were constructed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think both would be my answer because the social conditions to which you refer obtained not only in western Kosovo but in much of the Balkans, and yet these kulas were only built in that region. So in that sense it was a fashion, but, yes, there was a very practical purpose behind the fashion in that sense. If you've seen pictures of them you know that they are very imposing buildings, and so only wealthy families would afford them, for starters, but yes they had a practical purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's all for now. Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's time for rest, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Riedlmayer, my next question relates to your statement or your testimony given in the Milutinovic case. While you were cross-examined by my colleague Mr. Bakrac, he was particularly interested in the kulas that were demolished by the Albanians but which were owned by the Serbs. Do you know anything about this? Because from your answer given to my colleague Bakrac in the Milutinovic case, I couldn't quite gather what you meant. The reference page is 2704, line 10, I'm talking about Kula Kusko [Realtime transcript read in error "Pusko"], Kos, Garica, Decani. Are you aware that these kulas have been demolished by the Albanians and that they were the property of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not kulas that I visited, and therefore I have no information about them. I'm not surprised that such things may have happened, but I have no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, line 22, instead of Kula "Pusko" it should read Kula "Kusko," with a K. [In English] Then Kos, K-o-s, yes. Then Garica. And last one is okay. It's okay, Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in the following: You mentioned in your report that Gracanica - and that was in the Milosevic case - that the famous Serbian monastery of Gracanica was a large military base. That's on page 2743. Do you have information about some other Orthodox shrines being used for these purposes? I know that you mentioned that at one point the troops, the army troops, were stationed or billeted in the St. Anton monastery, but do you have any accurate information about Islamic shrines being used as the basis for the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Albanian terrorists as the then-Yugoslav authorities used to call them?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I have no information about any use of houses of worship of the Islamic Community as a -- for military purposes. I couldn't obviously observe these during the war. What I did try to observe as we looked at damaged mosques is any signs that the building had been in the middle of some fire-fight. Usually when there is a fire-fight you would expect lots of bullet-holes in the building. And that was not common. More commonly you would see single catastrophic damage, like a large hole blasted in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit D004-2675 be called up. And we are going to see this whole document page by page, until the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the cover page of the book. You can see its title in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now quickly move to page 2. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see that this is a book published by the State Archive of Kosovo, the archive sector of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You see who was on the editorial board of this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please. Can we please zoom in to the photo along with the captions underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it looks like the mosque in Rogovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in only on the textual part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You can see what it says in English and the same reads in French, Serbian, and Albanian. It says that this is a mosque in Rogovo built in the sixteenth century and that in 1998 and 1999 it served as a KLA headquarter. This picture was taken in April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We also see who the publisher is. We don't need to enlarge this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is important because we have an ISBN number of the publisher on this page for the purpose of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as soon as we get the picture, I would like you to enlarge this particular line. That's right. Thank you. That would be all. Your Honours, I offer this document to be admitted into evidence. That's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And secondly, during the examination of Witness Sabri Popaj, while my colleague Aleksandar Popovic was doing the cross-examination, an identical photograph was marked for identification: D315. Now I tender this to be admitted into evidence because we have another confirmation by this witness that this is the mosque in Rogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think that's sufficient basis for the tendering of this exhibit into evidence, and I believe it had been marked for identification with an earlier witness. But I don't -- the witness has not been asked any questions except for one regarding that photograph. And I don't believe it's sufficient for the tendering of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Isn't it a photograph that features in the evidence-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And on what basis then do you object to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't object to the page with the photograph. I understand my learned colleague wants to tender the entire publication, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it the whole book or the photograph that you are tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you look at the record, I was very accurate. I tendered the entire documentation shown to be admitted through this witness. So far we only had photograph that was marked for identification, and I tender it to be admitted into evidence because I think the conditions for that do exist. So I'm talking about the -- Sabri Popaj's evidence. Therefore, only photograph feature there, but with -- through this witness I would like to tender all these documents including the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But this witness has not been able to say anything about the document beyond recognising the photograph of the damaged mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely in dispute, whether this was actually the mosque in Rogovo or not. I do not object to the Chamber ruling on this later, but as far as this testimony is concerned, I tender this whole set of photographs given by the Defence under D004-2675 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view, Mr. Djordjevic, that the one page, the photograph of the mosque, could be received if you think it is to serve a purpose of the Defence. It is, of course, a duplication of a photograph that is presently marked for identification and it is, in my recollection, a photograph -- another copy of a photograph that is part of the evidence of the witness in chief. But if you see reason for that photograph that you have shown the witness to be received, we will receive it, but not the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no point in admitting only the photograph because this same photograph was used in examination-in-chief. It is important for me to admit either everything or nothing at all. Why? Because this was a publication published by the KLA which shows that this mosque was used as the main headquarters of the Kosovo Liberation Army. This is what their publication says. And for that reason I think it is significant for it to be admitted into evidence in its entirety because we maintain that this was the KLA headquarters and this is what the book says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer, I'm afraid, remains as it was, Mr. Djordjevic. The witness has not been able to speak about the book or that caption that you wanted. At some other time you may want to discuss with Ms. Kravetz whether she would agree to it or you may find a witness who's able to identify the book and say something of its authorship and reliability. But this witness has contributed nothing to that in his evidence and knowledge. Therefore, it's -- the only thing that we would admit is the photograph, and as you point out that's of no value because it's already in evidence as part of the evidence of this witness. So the -- nothing will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Actually, we dealt here with six pages from the book and the Defence wanted to offer evidence of the authenticity of this document and it was related to the question that I put to the witness, and that was whether he knows if any sacral buildings of the Islamic Community were used for military purposes as well. Therefore, the point of my putting this document to the witness was precisely that. But I will agree that there are other ways to have this kind of documents admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, my next question is the following. In your report you dealt with 607 mosques in Kosovo and Metohija. It seems to me that you mentioned some information bases dating from 1997. First of all, can you tell me how did you acquire this information?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I believe the date was slightly earlier than that. I don't have my report in front of me, but it should be easy enough to check. The number of 607 mosques in Kosovo comes from a publication of the Islamic Community of Kosovo, their monthly entitled "Dituria Islame," that's D-i-t-u-r-i-a I-s-l-a-m-e, it means something like "Islamic knowledge." And it's an illustrated periodical with the usual expected religious content, but it also includes occasional articles about the history of the Islamic Community. And there was an article in it, I believe it was 1993, I'd have to check, that listed the numbers of mosques in Kosovo. 607 was the total number of existent mosques. The number that were in actual use were 463 or close to that. And this was with reference to the conclusion of our report that in excess of a third of all mosques in Kosovo suffered some degree of damage during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I still don't understand. There's a sentence in your report which literally reads, and it's 2.3, the damage of the Islamic heritage. Paragraph 2 reads as follows: "According to the statistical data published in 1993 ..." What kind of statistical data are you referring to? What's the source of this data?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just mentioned the source which was this monthly put out by the Islamic Community of Kosovo, which, as the central coordinating body of the Islamic Community in Kosovo, actually administered these mosques. If they put out figures in their publication, I assume that they have some basis for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but you say: "According to the statistical data published in 1993 ..." It is official government bodies that provide statistical data, not religious communities, that is why I'm asking you about the source. You say 1993 there were six or seven mosques --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak slowly when he's giving numbers and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking you again what sort of official statistical data did you acquire dating back from 1993, if you can give me an answer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It is not my understanding that statistical data have to emanate from a government body. In this case the body that actually operates and administers these mosques is the Islamic Community of Kosovo. I think they would have a basis for knowledge of how many mosques there really are under their control on a given date. And if they published that information, I assume that it can be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you assumed that one can rely on that. Did you collate this information with some other data and did you personally check the accuracy of the number of the mosques?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no means of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, did you use any information relating to Roman Catholic places of worship in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Roman Catholic community has a number of publications that deal with the history of the Roman Catholic community in Kosovo. It, however, did not include statistics of this kind. It also did not seem a particularly important figure to pursue, given that the damage to Roman Catholic monuments was relatively limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Apparently you didn't understand me. I asked you generally about the number of Roman Catholic shrines in Kosovo, not about the damage that they incurred, just the number. First I asked you about the Islamic ones. Now I'm asking you about Roman Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the numbers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever try to find out the number when you talked to Reverend Puka that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman was Ambroz Ukaj, and he was parish priest in Djakovica, and I inquired of him about the churches in his area of Djakovica. I had -- I made no inquiries with him about other parts of Kosovo. He did indicate that a number of the churches and villages around Djakovica had been damaged or destroyed during the war, and these are included in my database. I did, at a later point, stop in Prizren where the diocese of Kosovo is -- the Roman Catholic authorities in Kosovo are headquartered, and I asked there for information on damage to churches. I did not ask about the total number of churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about St. Anton church in Djakovica, you said that Father Ambroz Ukaj was all the time in Djakovica. You also said in your report that at one point the army vacated or evacuated the monastery and removed all the clergy in order for them to occupy the church for their own purposes. Did you discuss the consequences of the shelling of the nearby barracks that was close to the St. Anton church and how it all affected the church itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the whole purpose of my conversation with him, given that the allegation concerned damage to the church. And I first went and looked at the church and it had had the windows replaced, but otherwise was in an undamaged condition. And I asked him whether there had been any damage to the church. And he said, in fact, the NATO air-strike had not destroyed either the rectory or the church other than blowing out the windows; that the rectory had been used during the war by the Yugoslav Army; and that when he was finally able to take possession of the rectory again near the end of the war that there was damage to the rectory mainly from it being stripped of furniture, computers, and other equipment; and that it had been vandalised. But beyond that, he offered no assessment as to what the effects of the bombing were on that church.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a brief digression. When you say "vandalised," you mentioned computers and furniture, do you mean that they were looted, that the computers and some of the church furniture were looted?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he mentioned to me was that, first of all, the place had been looted; that all the contents basically were missing; that there were graffiti on the walls; and that the place had been smashed up, in his words. That's what.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you talked a lot about the damage of Islamic, as you say, cultural monuments, cultural monuments, I'm going to ask you about -- before we go back to the Islamic monuments, what you can tell us about the damage of the Serbian Orthodox heritage. This is the first question that I will put to you, generally.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the Serbian Orthodox heritage, you will note that our report has an entire section devoted to damage to Serbian Orthodox heritage in Kosovo. What we found was that there had been damage to approximately 80 churches in Kosovo. Some of these we visited ourselves. For others we obtained information primarily from the Serbian Orthodox Church authorities with whom we exchanged information and photographs. They used some of ours; we used some of theirs. We further found that the damage to Serbian Orthodox monuments occurred after the end of the war in June, primarily during the three months after the end of hostilities. By the time we arrived in October, attacks had diminished but they sporadically continued. And then, as we all know, in 2004 there were massive riots and some 30 further churches were vandalised or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This last thing you're thinking of the events of the 17th of March, 1994, I assume, in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 2004. Thank you. Can you please tell me how many locations of the Serbian Orthodox Church you toured during your first visit to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the number at my finger tips, but I believe it's mentioned in my report; if it's not, it should be easy enough to look up. We probably visited about a dozen in all. We kept the number fairly low because we already had access to documentation about destruction which the Serbian Orthodox Church had publicised, both on its web site and in an illustrated publication called "Raspeto Kosovo," Crucified Kosovo. Subsequent to that, a second augmented edition of the book came out the following year, and we also used that as well as other photographs that we obtained through correspondence with Father Sava Janjic. We did visit all of the churches concerning which there had been allegations about damage during the war, and we did visit all the main sites, such as the ones you mentioned earlier with reference to the World Heritage Sites to determine their condition. The places we did not visit were places that were more difficult to access since our time was limited and the roads were bad. So, for example, we did not visit the Orthodox monastery church at Musitiste, which is not far from Prizren but is down a very bad road and it would have taken us an extra day because there were more than half a dozen photographs of it already published on the Serbian Orthodox Church web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you visited or looked at the Serbian cemeteries around the large Kosovo cities, Pristina, Pec, Djakovica, or any other towns in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you will note, Your Honours, in the report in the introductory part we mention that we specifically excluded cemeteries and archaeological sites from our visit simply because, A, it would have added significantly to the time required; and B, because it would have been next to impossible to get comparative documentation as to what a cemetery might have looked like a year before the war and what it looked like after the war. So it was not part of our official survey. However, since you asked, yes, I did see some vandalised cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, can you please be more precise, Serbian population, Albanian, Catholic, Roman Catholic, some other?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw damage to cemeteries, both Serbian Orthodox and Muslim cemeteries. Since your question referred to Serbian Orthodox cemeteries, I saw damaged cemeteries near Mitrovica on my visit in 2001, that was the Serbian Orthodox cemetery on the southern edge of the town Mitrovica, gravestones had been overturned and it looked very thoroughly destroyed. There were others in western Kosovo where there were damaged Serbian Orthodox churches with cemeteries next to them with gravestones that had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, you visited 144 places in total. In those or out of those 144 places roughly, how many places were places of Islamic cultural heritage? We heard that there were about ten about -- related to the Serbian cultural heritage. I don't know if you refer to any numbers regarding the Roman Catholic, and how many then out of those would be related to the Islamic cultural heritage?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, correction, it was more than ten. I would say probably about 15. I said earlier a dozen, so -- but that's about the order of magnitude, about 10 per cent of the places we visited. In terms of the rest, I don't have the exact statistical breakdown. It may be mentioned in our report. It was ten years ago, so I don't have the figures in my head, although I once did. That includes not only Islamic but also historic residential architecture, general cultural institutions such as museums and libraries and so forth. So it's not that the remaining 90 per cent is all Islamic. It also, of course, includes the Catholic churches, of which I think we visited maybe half a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you visited about 120 monuments of Islamic architecture or cultural heritage, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems like an order of magnitude that's roughly correct. Taken in a very broad sense, so that includes things like not just mosques but Islamic schools, libraries, archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question relates to -- I mentioned one name. You said you never heard of that name in the context of your report and you were right. I apologise because of that. It is actually a person by the name of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the counsel said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
