utterances.text: -- and in your report in appendix 3 where you talk about allegations of the destruction of cultural heritage in Kosovo from 1998 to 1999, especially in relation to the -- those reported by Yugoslav cultural and other institutions, you said: "The presentation of the Yugoslav government reproduced by many international experts on cultural heritage without trying independently to check these claims the same allegations of the Yugoslav government by -- of damage inflicted on cultural monuments" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that there was a problem, that what I was doing seems to me I was doing too fast. So I'm going to repeat again: A presentation of the Yugoslav government. Then they reproduced -- which were reproduced by many international experts for the cultural heritage without an attempt to independently confirm these allegations. Those same allegations of the Yugoslav government about the damage inflicted on the cultural heritage were repeated also in the memorandum which the Prosecutor's Office of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia submitted -- or submitted to the Tribunal by Professor Mitchel [sic] and others about the alleged violations of international law by the governments and the officials of the NATO countries. First of all, do you know who Professor Mandel is? Secondly, what is being disputed in reference to these allegations? I know that you dealt with so-called false reports by the Yugoslav authorities on cultural monuments, but I would just like you to clarify what you said in your report.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. With reference to Professor -- it's not Mitchel, Michael Mandel, he is a professor of law at Osgoode Law School in Canada, and he took it upon -- Osgoode, that's O-s-g-o-o-d-e, hall, okay. He took it upon himself to organise an informal tribunal held in New York. This informal tribunal was to judge war crimes allegedly committed by NATO in its war against Yugoslavia in 1999. And what I referred to is that as part of its conclusions, this ad hoc tribunal accepted in its whole the allegations that were published in the Yugoslav government White Book. And once it reached its conclusions, it forwarded them to the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. I don't know what, if any, follow-up there was thereafter. But the ad hoc tribunal had no official standing of any sort, and it seemed to be convened for certain purposes of the participants, not by any official body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: You wrote in your report that there were about 210 Serbian Orthodox churches in Kosovo. Is this, roughly speaking, the number that you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 210 was the figure that was mentioned in the publication of the Republican Institute for the Protection of Monuments as being architecturally significant, culturally significant Orthodox sites in Kosovo. Obviously that does not include any number of village churches of recent vintage. That would not have made it into a publication of the Institute for the Protection of Monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. You have clarified a lot with this answer. Are you familiar with the actual number of Orthodox places of worship in Kosovo, not just those of cultural, religious, or any other kind of special value, but just any church? Do you know or did you get from the patriarchate of the Serbian Orthodox Church, i.e., Father Sava Janjic, the correct total number of Serbian Orthodox churches in Kosovo and did you receive such information? Were you interested in this type of information at all, first of all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interested -- I'm sorry. I should slow down. I was interested in the information, but I was not able to obtain a clear figure. The problem is that in all of the official publications of the Yugoslav heritage authorities and of the Serbian Orthodox Church, there is no distinction made in the compilations between churches that are active, functioning places of worship, and churches that may be only foundations or mentioned in medieval chronicles and no longer existent at all. If one includes all of the churches that ever existed in Kosovo; for example, there was a book edited by Gojko Subotic called something like, "Kosovo: The Sacred Land," he lists over a thousand places, but many of these are archaeological sites or merely churches that once existed of which no trace remains above ground. So I had great difficulty in nailing down the figure. As far as my communications with Father Sava were concerned, Father Sava was famous for being the cyber monk. He was the only Orthodox church official in Kosovo to have access to the internet at this crucial period. And it was very difficult to get through to him. So our exchanges with him were largely confined to things like exchanging pictures. Later on, when internet communication improved, the communications had to do with reconstruction projects. And so I did not further pursue the question of statistics. The statistics on the Islamic Community were included largely because they were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I hope I will be forgiven if I call the Serbian Orthodox Church Eparchy by its wrong name, but I think it's called the Raska Prizrenska Eparchy. Any way, what you -- I believe that they have detailed information about the Orthodox places of worship and shrines in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. So, again, I'm asking you if you requested such information from the Raska Prizrenska Eparchy.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our focus was not on conducting a census of churches, but on determining what had been damaged. And I think in that our figures match very closely what the Orthodox Eparchy of Raska and Prizren has itself published concerning damage to its properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you were aware of the problem that all localities of the Serbian Orthodox Church were ghettos that were forbidden. Not even the faithful could go there during the war or immediately after the war or move there safely. Do you have information about that? This also means that the Orthodox priests could not have precise information about the damage inflicted on the property of the Serbian Orthodox Church. I don't know if you are informed about this, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, we followed up on these contacts with the Orthodox church ourselves; and by the time we submitted our report in the summer of 2001, there were no more surprises about what had or had not been damaged in Kosovo, although security conditions especially in the first year or two after the war were difficult. I know for a fact that Father Sava travelled with KFOR military escort to virtually every place in Kosovo that had or once had a Serb population. And so every time new information emerged, it was posted on his web site and we would add it to our report. I'm not aware that in the intervening years there have been any more revelations about things that were damaged in 1999 that we did not know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is unusual, strange, because you mentioned on several occasion false reporting by the Yugoslav authorities about damage inflicted to a property of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Kosovo. So it seems strange that you did not yourself personally try to check information, even the information that was not accessible, about the status of Serbian Orthodox monuments in Kosovo because the number of protected churches, 210, represents one-third of all the total number of mosques, those of cultural significance, smaller, minor cultural significance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite sure what the counsel is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're reading far too quickly and it's -- the interpreter is having to indicate that they cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to apologise. I was not reading, I was speaking, so -- but it was a little bit fast. And I am going to try to repeat my question and make it as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The number of churches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you notice at all the transcript of what you describe as your questions? These are relatively short on the current page and they go for seven, eight, nine, ten lines, the short ones. You're having more of a debate than a question-and-answer session, I suspect. If you could try short questions, short propositions, the interpreters would find it easier and the witness may be able to answer more directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm going to try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Why did the witness pay attention to of all the other cultural monuments in Kosovo, 80 per cent of the monuments of Islamic culture, and another percentage of the Roman Catholic monuments; but the real situation on the ground is not like that. The real situation is that there are a greater number of Christian places of worship in Kosovo and Metohija than generally Serbian -- or Muslim ones. And so why did he pay more attention to the Islamic monuments and only, let's say, 20 per cent of the Christian monuments is the reason for that, his interest in the Islamic culture. And is that something that the witness can agree with me and is that something that is in his report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, our focus on what had been destroyed in the war and in its immediate aftermath. To that extent we believe that our report is substantially complete. It covers all the sites, regardless of its ethnic or religious background that were reported to have been damaged during the war. It includes information not only from our personal site visits, but based on documentation from all sources that we considered reliable, whether it was the religious communities, the EU/IMG report, the monuments authorities, or other sources. I don't think it is fair to suppose that there should be, you know, some sort of question of pre-determined proportions. We were not going down a list of churches or mosques and checking off which ones were damaged and which ones were not. Our focus was in following up allegations. And it is, I think, a reasonable supposition, given that there are so many interested parties involved, the communities who had the care of these buildings, that any damage that did occur would have produced an allegation. I hope that answers your question. Finally, with regard to the Yugoslav government allegations, we did, in fact, follow-up every single allegation in the Yugoslav government White Book by actually visiting those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that I'm not fully satisfied with your answer, but at the end I have to conclude, and you will agree with me hopefully, that your job was, in fact, to verify the allegations of, as you call them, interested parties relating to the accusations that their property suffered damage; and that your mission was not intended to provide an objective picture of the totality of the damage to the cultural heritage in Kosovo, irrespective of any reports, either official or unofficial. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not. We did, in fact, make a good-faith effort to verify reports. First of all, by doing percentage check of places on which documentation had been provided, and also by compiling a list of places for which there were allegations and then checking them against our own observations. We found no sites for which the religious communities in particular had claimed damage where there was no damage. Often the degree of damage was exaggerated or imperfectly stated. But when the Islamic Community or the Orthodox community claimed that the site had been damaged, it usually was -- in fact, it always was. Now, as to corroborating allegations, we did not include in our report any allegations for which there was not corroborating evidence in the form of photographs and by independent other sources which confirmed the allegation. So it was not merely a question of compiling various accusations, it was a good-faith effort to determine to the best of our limited abilities what the situation on the ground was. If you are aware of significant destruction that we missed, I would be very interested in knowing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I understand you, you and Mr. Herscher started your job immediately upon receiving information that huge damage was inflicted on the cultural heritage in Kosovo, and as an expert you felt it your duty to react. After all this vandalism and devastation and razing to the ground of many Serbian monasteries relating to the events of the 17th of April, 2004, did you feel that your duty was to inform the world public about what had happened to this particular segment of the cultural heritage of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will check the updated copy of my resume, you will see that I collaborated with Cultural Heritage Without Borders in their report on the damage to Serbian Orthodox heritage in the March 2004 riots. So I had the interest, but I didn't have the funding to go out and start a new field research. Besides, there were other parties already engaged in that. The reason for undertaking our 1999 survey was precisely the information that it seemed like there was no one else trying to do that kind of work at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree, but as His Honour Judge Parker said, it is not my place to debate these issues with you. Can you tell me, please, did you verify the facts stated by Mr. Bajgora, the then-deputy of the mufti of the Islamic Community in Kosovo relating to the book referred to in your report entitled: Serbian Barbaric Acts Against the Albanian Heritage in Kosovo? Did you address this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the book. I have seen it. The photos published in the book are all photos that I already had, so our report is not based on that report -- on that book. Other than that, I cannot really characterise the text part of the book. I did not read it very carefully. It seemed in the same general tone as the publications of the Serbian Orthodox Church complaining about the ways in which it felt itself to have been victimised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, please, Mr. Feiz Drancoli [phoen], he was the director of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments of Kosovo and you had a working relationship with him, didn't you? I don't know his last name, whether it's Trancoli or Drancoli, but first name Feiz.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Drancoli.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you visited with him Junik and Rogovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, he came with us on one of the days that we went out on the tour, and we visited a large number of sites in Pec, in Drsnik, Gjakova, Junik, Rogovo, a number of places -- no, wait a minute, I'm not sure he was with us in Rogovo, but in western Kosovo anyway. And his function largely was to act as a guide. Some of these places like Nivokaz, which I just mentioned, are on unmarked roads and would have been hard for us to find. He was familiar with the sites. He would show us where things were. He had no input on our assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were dealing with the consequences but at the same time with the causes of damage, when you visited Junik and Rogovo did you hear from any witness that the KLA headquarters used to be there?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any such information. In the case of Junik, of course, it's well-known from news reports that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question refers particularly to the witnesses that you've spoken to, but thank you anyway for this answer. You said that the Institute for the Protection of Culture and Monuments of Kosovo lost its archive because in 1999, during the withdrawal of the army and the police of Yugoslavia under the Kumanovo Agreement from Kosovo in June, the entire archive of the Institute for the Protection of Culture and Monuments was transferred to Serbia. Is that correct? Are you familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, in view of the nature of your job and your interest in Kosovo, did you visit Serbia to review the archive of the Institute for the Protection of Culture and Monuments of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next set of my questions will refer to a couple of things that we discussed yesterday, primarily the part that relates to the questions put to you by His Honour Judge Parker, namely, this was about the photographs that you provided the OTP from the allegedly known sources immediately before this trial began and this was in July. I'm talking about specifically the mosque in Cirez. Did you ever visit this mosque yourself? Let us be very accurate and specific. Did you see it with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove by it on a return to Pristina from a day's surveying. It was late, it was dark, and we did not stop. I did not include it among the sites personally visited because I did not stop to make a survey, but I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course you know where it is, that's understandable, but you said that it was dark while you were passing by the mosque. Were you able to see the mosque in the dark, or were you not able to see it at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it from the road. It's visible from the road, but I did not stop to make a survey, in part because there was no possibility of making photographs. As you will see, however, there are -- the photographs I have are from multiple sources, including the EU/IMG survey. They have a photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you already explained and I'm not going to ask you any further questions about this; however, from the photographs that we have seen - and I don't think it's necessary for us to see them again, it's already admitted into evidence, it's P0133. We all perfectly well remember these photographs we saw yesterday. Quite simply, when you look at these three domes and this large arch, I have no way of comparing them with the previously early -- existing mosque in Cirez. In other words, I was not even able to find any locations that would give me some bench-marks indicating that we are talking about the same site. I don't know if you went into this problem at any length, and if you have nothing to say about this it's okay. I'm not going to press the matter.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you brought it up, I was interested enough after yesterday's event to take another look at the photographs. And if they could be shown on the monitor I could point out something that I noticed on a second look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, are you wanting that to be done now or are you watching time very closely?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am watching the time, and perhaps it would be better that we deal with this after the break because this is a separate subject that I have for this witness and I'm definitely going to finalise my cross-examination today. Maybe we can take a break earlier and then finish earlier, before we move to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a break now and resume in half an hour at ten minutes to 1.00. And it may be possible, Mr. Djordjevic, if you coordinate with the Court Officer to ensure and the right exhibits are ready to be displayed. We'll have a further break now, Mr. Riedlmayer, and resume in half an hour's time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that final session should be the end of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we, please, now have on our screens an exhibit that is already in evidence, that's P01132 MFI. These are, in fact, two photographs on pages 2 and 3, and if we can have them juxtaposed on the screen together -- actually, only the upper photograph, not the lower one. If I understand correctly, this is being done at the request of Mr. Riedlmayer because he wanted to provide some additional information if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And I believe that this is what you actually wanted to see, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the photographs I wanted because I was not satisfied with the photographs that I already had; they didn't show the building from comparable angles. This one is comparable. Would you like me to comment on it? What I noticed, Your Honours, is, as you may recall yesterday there was a question of how a mosque with a ground floor and an upper floor suddenly is reduced to only the arcade with the back missing and the three domes resting atop the arcade. And the question was: Is this a different mosque? And my surmise was that the arcade had simply collapsed, I mean -- I'm sorry, the storey on top of the arcade has simply collapsed from the blast. What I noticed upon examining these photos again last night in my room is something that I failed to point out yesterday. Namely, if you look at the left-hand photo which is a relatively recent photo and look carefully under the left-hand small dome you can see a bit of the sky. And I don't know if it's possible to zoom in at all, but I could see the contrast both by zooming in. And by darkening the photo, you can see that that is not an element of the building under the dome that is actually a bit of the sky. And what you can also see is, in front of the three domes that are in a very unusual uncharacteristic pattern of the front dome -- of the central dome being in front of the two sides domes, there are remnants of two supporting columns. And if you look at the two -- in the pre-war photo in the same positions you can see the concrete columns that support the roof and the second storey right above the central arcade. And I believe those are the stubs. So my explanation for this photo is -- I mean, for the damage is that a rather large blast levelled the main prayer hall of the mosque, the space under the large dome, and in the process also blew out the superstructure, the upper storey above the arcade. And that the three small domes which is are prefabricated simply landed on the vacated space. For this it's also useful to understand what the structure is made of. Basically it's a concrete skeleton and the red material is very light, hollow brick. So that would very easily be affected by such a blast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Is there more you wish to ask, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, can we reduce the left-hand photograph to its original size. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, this photograph taken before the war of this mosque and the photograph on the left, do you know the exact dates when these pictures were taken? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic, I do know them. The photograph on the right was taken during the Bajram in 1998, that is April of 1998. In the photograph below it you can actually see the overflow congregation in front of the mosque performing the holiday prayer. The photograph on the left was taken in July, this year, by Mr. Hamiti when he took the trip from Pristina to Cirez.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And the other one was taken in 2000 and?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other one, the pre-war picture, was taken in 1998. And the post-war picture is from 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 2009. Thank you. All I can see in this photograph is that the overhead power line run in a totally different direction compared to the pre-war one, but let's go back to the first photograph. So let's keep the photograph on the left taken in 2009 and instead of the one which is actually number 2 can we have photograph number 1 from the same exhibit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to zoom in the central part of photograph number 1 where you can see two open windows which actually look onto a house and there is a car there too. So a little more to the right, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph we can see a building relatively close to this building that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please zoom out now to have the photograph back to its original size. We can also see a kind of vehicle there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If we were to accept that this was the same building, it could have been photographed, if we look at the left-hand side from the direction of the smaller electrical pole that we see. This is what it seems to look like. However, closer where we see this bigger electrical pole, we don't see the house that we were able to see through the openings in this other photograph, it's missing, although it was a new house. We can see that it has a roof and everything. So this also is something that throws some doubt on exactly what happened. I noticed that the domes are absolutely undamaged on the left photograph in comparison to the photograph on the right. There is also an arch here which we did not see on any of the photographs that were showing the mosque. So can you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. First of all, note that the photograph on the left was taken ten years after the photograph on the right. The photograph on the right was taken in the summer of 1999. Secondly, you will note that the alignment of the three domes matches your surmise, namely, that the view is from the rear of the building, from the distant power pole because the central dome is forward of the two side domes. What you will also note is that in the very recent photo the concrete domes are absolutely bare. The metal cladding has been taken off. It's essentially aluminum sheeting. And what is damaged in the photo at right is the aluminum sheeting which has been removed. As you noted when you zoomed in there were a lot of loose hollow bricks. You will note that in the post-war photo of 2009 all the hollow bricks have been cleared away, presumably because they were reusable. So my only explanation for the missing building and missing car is that both the car and the building have left the scene in the last ten years. I also have other photos which I did not bring into court because they were somewhat duplicative, but showing the same scene from a broader angle. A new mosque has been rebuilt to the left of the ruined one, with the ruins left intact. And so there have been some alterations to the scene; in a ten-year period that is not unusual. The house that you see looks like a very odd building, and it's -- although it has a roof, it seems to be missing its windows. So I assume that like the hollow bricks from the ruined mosque, it too was carted away. That's the only thing. Now, as to the arch-like structure. It is in my view actually present in the 2009 picture. If you look carefully under the left-hand dome you can see some trace of it. What it is it's not an arch; it's essentially a stiff structure, something like metal or tar paper. If you still have the other photos from -- the ones from my database that were exhibited, they show it very clearly hanging from the side in that picture we had yesterday, the one that viewed the building from the side. What it was is the internal section of the roof that supported the large dome of the mosque. It's now been cut in half and it's hanging down. But the fact that you can see the sky underneath the dome on the left, in the 2009 picture, to me indicates that that dome is not in its original position, that it is very plausible that its support has been knocked out and it simply landed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is all at the level of an assumption, and we can all agree with that. However, this photograph that was taken immediately after the destruction of the mosque where we see the damaged domes, a vast majority of material that should still be there from the part that had fallen through should in any case be visible on the ground. However, the parts that we see are mainly parts of the armature. They're not the hollow bricks. There's simply a lot of material that is missing which we should be able to see as the photograph was taken shortly after the mosque was destroyed in 1999. Can you please deal a little bit more with this point.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What we're looking at is the interior of the entrance facade which would have been relatively shielded. It still has the roof of the first -- of the ground floor on it. If you look at the -- I don't know if we can get those exhibits back, but the two pictures that were in my database --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe they're coming up now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. The photograph you see on top there - I don't know if it's possible to zoom in - okay the photograph you see on top, it is my contention that was taken from the right side of the mosque. So if you were facing the mosque directly towards the entrance, it would be the right side of the building. And so what I believe you are seeing here is that red stiff structure is the base of the dome that's hanging down and looking like an arch in the other picture which was taken from the right-hand side, from where you see that rubble. And so there is plenty of rubble to be seen, but the main part of the mosque that collapsed was the part to the right of the little dome and that's where you would expect to see the rubble. There is also rubble in front of the mosque which I believe may be that second storey that was blown out when the mosque was destroyed. Of the three domes, all you can see is the profile of the far right one because it is taken directly from the right-hand side. You can see behind it perhaps -- no -- well, what you can see on top of it is a little bit of that peeled-away aluminum sheeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to zoom in on the top photograph only, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On this photograph we see one dome with some damage on it. We can see that it is covered with aluminum. However, I cannot say or agree that the other two domes are visible. In view of the configuration that they were in, at least one of them would be in -- would be visible. They were asymmetrical. One of them was in front and the two were behind. So this photograph actually creates even more doubt in my mind as to the authenticity of the material you provided. And also, the fact is that none of these red walls is visible on any of the photographs, especially not from these construction materials. And the photographs were taken approximately around the same time in 1999, after they were destroyed. So I don't even see the arches here. I don't see any part of the concrete construction. And the details that we see on the other photographs were exclusively made out of cement. They do have some brickwork and tiles on the roof, but this creates a problem for me. We see a woods -- wood behind the building. We see a large tree to the right. We see the power transmission lines, how they lie. So, I mean, really, if you have any other comments I would like to hear it, but I have not managed to convince myself that it is actually exactly that same building.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm sorry for the bad resolution on this. Because it's in the database, it had to be kept low. But you can, if you look very carefully, see another dome to the right of the one, just the lower part of it. And the reason you don't see the middle dome, at least not obviously here, is because the photograph is not directly level with the domes but slightly from the rear of the building. So what you see is the two rear domes, the two flanking domes, one very clearly with the peeled-up metal sheeting and the other one behind it. Now, as for the red, the red is the tar paper roof basically. And you see it in the black-and-white photograph not from the side but from the rear of the building, and the reason it looks like an arch is because it had a big circle cut out for it for the main dome. And here you can see it collapsed. You can see other parts of it lying on the ground. But the part that is attached to the partially intact part of the building is hanging down, which is why it forms an arch in the black-and-white photo. I think there is plenty of construction material to be seen here, and the concrete elements you refer to are the same ones you can see in the pre-war photos. The window at the left and -- is the window at the side of the front arcade, which is also visible in the post-war photo. The reason you cannot see the woods in the distance in any of the pre-war photos is none of the pre-war photos were from this angle. The people praying were on the other side of the mosque and then the only other angles we had is a view directly towards the entrance and a view from the rear towards the entrance. So you never had this angle before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect that we have exhausted what can be said and viewed about this. Thank you both. And we will consider --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, Your Honour. You are correct. The house is missing here which could be seen before. A lot of that is still in doubt. But anyway, I will continue with my questions, and I will bring my cross-examination slowly to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would be interested in the following: Do you have the statistical data regarding the mosques that were presented to you by the Prosecutor and which you also discussed in your report, do you have records of how many places in a municipality you visited? This is how I'm going to put this question to you. I'm not going to ask you about it in another way.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a statistical breakdown by municipality, but with the use of my database it would be very easy to establish. But it would take a bit of time. I'm not sure what the -- what you are trying to find out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not trying, but I would wish to find out how many places you interpreted the data from without actually visiting these places, where you reached your conclusions on the basis of photographs. Because we are talking about a mosque which could be of a later date, if it is the same mosque at all. Anyway, the question has to do with the overall report of yours. I would like you just to tell us, out of these 144 locations that are covered in your report, how many of those locations did you actually visit; or, if you prefer, how many of those locations did you actually not visit?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The 144 locations that you mention are the locations we actually visited. The report covers a great many more places than that. So we visited 144 of the sites that are documented in the report. If you wish, I can point out on a map of Kosovo where we went, but basically we covered the larger part of the area of Kosovo, the places where we did not go tended to be places far from the main highways and where communications were difficult. We also didn't go to the far northern end of Kosovo, to Leposavic, because there had been no allegations of damage to cultural property up there. So Mitrovica is as far north as we went. But we went to south-east Kosovo, to west Kosovo, central Kosovo, the north, Prizren. We covered a lot of area. For places that we did not visit, we relied on photographs, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But that was not my question. You already talked about the things that you -- the locations that you visited in your report, so evidently I cannot get the answer to the question that I am putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, I would like to see P0111 [as interpreted], that exhibit on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will see this is the white mosque in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see in the transcript that it is -- in the transcript there are only three 1s, one 1 is missing, there should be four 1s. Can we look at this top photograph. I think that is the mosque that we are interested in. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about it so I'm not going to dwell on what you talked about. Can you please tell me, the source of information as to the manner of the damage of this mosque is just the report from the people you received on the ground, the people from the Islamic Community, or are there any other reports about the damage that you looked at in the case of this particular mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the manner of the damage is something we determined through first-hand inspection. As I explained in direct examination, we went inside the mosque, outside the mosque, looked at the type of damage to the minaret, and concluded from that how the minaret was damaged, namely, an explosion was set off inside the minaret. And the rest of the damage can largely be explained by the falling of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of allegations of the Yugoslav authorities that NATO bombed the OUP Suva Reka and that one bomb fell in the immediate vicinity of this mosque and that it was damaged by it? Did you find out about this? Just answer briefly.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't comment on this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I remember that there was such a thing in the White Book because we did the entire section of the two White Books published by the Yugoslav authorities that dealt with cultural property. What we did note is that the kind of damage seen here is not consistent with the mosque having been hit by any projectile from the outside. The blast came from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that you didn't have any technical knowledge and that you are making some conclusions on the basis of common sense, and that in some cases this was the only criteria for your assessments and evaluation. Did you engage any experts, technical experts, to help you to assess the damage of this mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did no technical testing. However, as I showed in the direct examination, the pattern of damage to the mosque was such that even without technical testing you could tell that the base of the minaret had ballooned outwards and that elements of it were sticking out by 10, 20, 30 centimetres. And consider that we have a pre-war photo on this same page of the minaret taken from the side and -- I cannot imagine a scenario - and I admit I'm not a military expert - where munitions would travel through the minaret to the base before setting off this huge blast which blew apart the minaret's base. It just doesn't seem to make sense to me. I've seen in the process of my report on Kosovo but also in subsequent reports in Bosnia literally hundreds of buildings that have been damaged by various means. And I would still say in retrospect, with the knowledge that I now have, the same thing, that this minaret was blown up from within and not the result of some projectile hitting it. Beyond that, all you have is the informant reports which we have discussed already. So I see no need to repeat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you allowed yourself to deal with something that you should not have really been dealing with because you are not an expert, but let us quickly move to the following topic and then after that to the last topic, after which I'm going to complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to look on the -- see on the screen something that has already been admitted into evidence, and this is P01109. Can we zoom in on this photograph, please. Can we please zoom in on the top part of the photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is, you would agree with me, the library of the Hadum mosque, the Sulejman Efendi Hadum mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There was some talk about it being damaged in a fire just like the rest of the old city centre around it and close to it, but we can see that the walls are completely white towards the floor and that the building is halved practically. So it does not seem to me that there was a fire here. What did you say yesterday relating to the reasons and the causes of damage of this library?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Consider that the library is a building composed mostly of masonry. The wooden elements were relatively small. They consisted of the floor which supported the upper story which you see here. It's the upper storey that had the book niches and windows. You cannot see it very well on this photo, but you can see, if you look carefully, a dark line at the bottom of the place where the floor was. What that was was charred wooden elements of the floor still sticking out from the wall. You can also see at the left-hand wall a niche. These were the niches that held the book-shelves, and once again there are charred book-shelves in there. If the library, as is alleged from various accounts and as also we can see from that aerial photo that I showed -- that I commented on during the direct examination, if the library was burned in March and then the library cut in half by the falling minaret in May, this whole interior would have been exposed to the elements for a period of approximately five months after the minaret fell on it. Now, I know for a fact that the minaret did fall on it, A, because I observed pieces of the minaret, identifiable as such, in the rubble when I first personally inspected the building in October of 1999, but also, since as you know, I and Mr. Herscher were involved in the post-war reconstruction of the Hadum mosque. We actually went to the scene in October of 2000 and went through the rubble and found identifiable elements of the balcony of the minaret, carved panels, which have been used in the restoration as models for the replacement. So I don't think there is a great deal of doubt that what cut this building in half was the top of the minaret which fell on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you to your answer. Still, I still don't see the tar and the soot that we would be seeing on the walls --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down and repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 11th and the 15th of April there was a bombing that damaged the library and the Hadum mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there are allegations in -- by the Yugoslav government that the Hadum mosque was damaged by bombardment. All I can speak to is what I observed and the conclusions I can draw from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with your conclusions. The only thing that I'm interested in is your conclusion regarding the allegation by Yugoslav authorities, and perhaps you will agree with me if I were to say that you think that this as a consequence of the NATO bombing is something that is absolutely ruled out as a cause from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree that I do not believe this to be the result of an air attack, neither the damage to the mosque nor the damage to the library. But as you will note, I was not present when the destruction occurred, so the conclusions I draw are limited by the evidence of the damage that I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you once more, did you use services of military experts when you drew up your findings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No need to ask the question, Mr. Djordjevic. We understand from the witness without hesitation that he sought no expert assistance. So to save you time, you don't need to ask again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. I have concluded my cross-examination with this. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no questions in re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I refer you to a photograph you took showing a mosque classified in the top damaged category. I think it was taken in October 1999. Now, you also encircled a brown and yellow building that was, you said, close to the mosque and that building was intact.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, can you give us some idea what was the distance between that building and the mosque?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say we are dealing with a building that is at least a hundred metres if not more removed in the background. The empty field of rubble you see in that photo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS JANOS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- consisted not only of the site of the mosque but also of the shops of an Albanian bazaar that surrounded it. It was the entire walk around there, surrounded on three sides by modern buildings that was demolished. The modern buildings were intact. Some of the modern buildings were quite close to the mosque, much closer than the building in the background. I marked that merely so you could understand how the mosque appeared. If you wish, I can point it out on the screen but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: There's no need. There's no need. Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, Mr. Riedlmayer, that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber is appreciative indeed of the assistance you have been able to give, the time you've spent here, and we're grateful that you've been able, again, to come to The Hague. Thank you very much for those matters. You may now, of course, go back to your other activities. You go with our thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before we conclude today, I just wanted to make an application regarding one of the last -- actually, the last exhibit I used with this witness yesterday, this is P1137. We have just been able to locate a colour version of that exhibit. The version I used yesterday was a black-and-white one, and the photographs there were not as clear as in the colour versions. I would just ask your leave to replace the version currently in e-court with that coloured version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not in e-court yet I take it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is, I'm sorry, and I didn't mention the name -- the number of the exhibit is P1137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's the black-and-white?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the colour in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, no, no. We can either attach it to the back or replace the version in e-court, as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The colour photograph may be added to the present exhibit. Don't delete what's there; add is our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to tell shortly, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Another matter, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- the photographs that were being discussed, the four -- the set of four photographs of the Cirez mosque, this is P1132 marked for identification, I would seek to tender those photographs into evidence given the extensive cross-examination on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is conscious that there's a deal of evidence to be considered about these exhibits, but in view of the adherence of the witness to his opinion, the Chamber would receive those exhibits in evidence, and in due course will reach its findings as to the subject matter of those photographs and whether or not it is in a position to accept the opinion of the expert about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the -- those marked for identification will now become exhibits with the same number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: One unrelated matter concerns next week's witness scheduling, and I just wanted to inquire with the Court regarding our scheduling -- our sitting time for Wednesday afternoon. It was my understanding that originally Wednesday afternoon was suspected to be a shorter sitting day, but we saw on the court calendar circulated yesterday that it's now -- we're now scheduled to sit up until 7.00 p.m. And we just wanted to confirm that that was the case. And I should point out the reason I'm bringing this up is because we have two witnesses next week as you know. Both of them will not be able to return to the Tribunal for testimony beyond next week, and we would really try to -- we will make our utmost effort to try to complete the testimony of both of those witnesses next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: More than one comment needs to be made, Ms. Kravetz. First, the Chamber observes that there have been now a growing number of witnesses in which it has been -- in respect of which it has been said, Well, the witness now has to leave so the time available for evidence must be curtailed. The Chamber - and I'm sure Defence counsel with us - try to accommodate the other commitments of witnesses, and that will be so next week with these witnesses. But if it does not prove possible to adequately deal with the evidence of those two witnesses in the time that they presently plan to make themselves available, then it will be necessary for that -- arrangements to be made for one or other of those witnesses to return at an appropriate time to finish their evidence. While all, I'm sure, endeavour to meet with and cooperate with their commitments, we've got to ensure that there's an adequate time available for the evidence. And if that isn't happening in a case, the matter must be dealt with by the witness coming back. As for the sitting next week, I have not seen the latest programme that you've mentioned, but our order has been that we will commence sitting at 1.30 on Wednesday. We did that in the understanding that there -- the courtroom is needed late in the day for another matter. Whether or not that is still the case, I do not know, but we will retain our commencement at 1.30, following the Judges' Plenary meeting, which is commencing at 9.00. And that may then provide a means of ensuring that we can finish the evidence of both witnesses. We will, of course, expect the Prosecution and the Defence to be extremely attentive to relevance with respect to both witnesses, in the hope that indeed their evidence can finish next week. Three full days for these two witnesses ought to be feasible if attention is paid to relevance and questions are directed to the important issues. But it could be that some extra time will be available on the Wednesday with the sitting commencing at 1.30, depending on something I do not presently know, whether or not another matter will continue in the courtroom late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems that you already said everything that I intended to say, and I hope that the OTP would have the similar understanding when our case starts. We have postponed some of the witnesses, and we are prepared to work full time. This will not present a problem but within the limits of our capabilities. However, lots depends on how we are going to work on Wednesday. The explanation that this witness can only come now and never again, I don't think that, as you said, is something that is subject to discussion. A witness must be available to the court whenever the Court decides, so I'm not going to comment on this any further. Once I receive information about what is going to happen on Wednesday, I will take the liberty to address my learned friends from the OTP if there are any problems. But in any case, you can count on the Defence to do their best to maintain and put into practice this agreement that we have just reached. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. In part, of course, it is the fact that we have arranged not to sit on Thursday and Friday to allow counsel to return to their homes, which puts us under a time pressure of those three days only next week. So we would expect full cooperation in an endeavour to finish the evidence of those two witnesses. We can now adjourn for the weekend and look forward to seeing you refreshed on Monday for the last three days of this term. And I believe on Monday we commence at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
